text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Picture a summer evening in a lakeside resort town. People are wandering down the main street after dinner. There's a shop with its door propped open, the smell of chocolate and fresh waffle cones drifting out, a queue for ice cream, and someone at the counter buying a box of fudge to take home to their neighbours.

speaker: JAMES
text: And behind that cosy scene is a surprisingly hard business problem. How much fudge do you make? How many tubs of each ice cream flavour do you need for tonight, and for the rainy Tuesday next week when the street is empty? And if you're the company that supplies dozens and dozens of these shops, how do you plan production for all of them at once?

speaker: NORA
text: That's the puzzle at the heart of our final company in this series.

speaker: JAMES
text: Our final company. It's strange to say that.

speaker: NORA
text: It is. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. This series has followed the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today, for episode thirty, it's Kilwins, the chocolate, fudge, ice cream and confectionery franchise headquartered in Petoskey, Michigan.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: franchise trade press, local news, the private equity firm's announcement and some industry sources. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number comes from the company, we'll flag it. And nothing here is investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I want to be especially upfront today. Kilwins is one of the thinnest public records we've worked with in the whole series. We don't have a confirmed founding year, a named chief executive, revenue, or even a total store count from our sources. And we found no evidence at all of Kilwins using AI. So today is as much about the industry, the customer and the opportunity as about the company itself, and we'll say plainly what isn't publicly known.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is its own kind of interesting. So what's the one-line version?

speaker: JAMES
text: Kilwins is a franchisor of shops selling chocolates, fudge, ice cream and other confections, based in northern Michigan, growing into new states like Texas and Arizona, voted the number one dessert chain by USA TODAY readers in June 2026, and owned by Levine Leichtman since February 2023.

speaker: NORA
text: And at the end of the episode, we'll step back and look at all thirty companies together.

speaker: JAMES
text: We will. But first, fudge.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with what we do know. Where is Kilwins?

speaker: JAMES
text: Headquarters is in Petoskey, Michigan, a small town on Lake Michigan in the northern part of the state's lower peninsula. If you don't know the area, it's a classic summer resort region, lakes, beaches, holiday homes, small towns with walkable main streets. That's relevant, because it's exactly the kind of setting where a fudge and ice cream shop thrives.

speaker: NORA
text: And Petoskey isn't just an office.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. In August 2026, a local news station reported that Kilwins had resumed tours in Petoskey and debuted a new exclusive waffle cone. Tours suggest there's a production facility people can visit. Kilwins is generally described as being backed by central production, meaning a significant part of what's sold in the shops is made centrally and supplied to the stores. We couldn't open the company's own pages to confirm the details of what's made where, so I'll keep that general.

speaker: NORA
text: Why would a confectionery company run tours?

speaker: JAMES
text: In our view, it's smart brand-building. Tours turn the production facility into an attraction in a tourist region, they reinforce the idea that the product is made with care, and they give visitors a story to take home. Launching an exclusive waffle cone at the same moment, in the peak of summer, gives local press a reason to cover it. It's a small example of how much of this business is about experience and storytelling, not just product.

speaker: NORA
text: How old is the company?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't confirm a founding year. There's a regional publication headline from August 2026, "75 years of fabulous fudge", which might refer to a Kilwins anniversary, but we didn't read the article, so we can't say for sure what it's counting from. What's clear from the press coverage is that this is a long-established, heritage brand, often called a legacy brand in franchise trade headlines.

speaker: NORA
text: Size?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not found, in terms of total stores, employees or revenue. Franchise directory sites list Kilwins, but we didn't read them. What we do have is a growth figure. QSR Magazine reported that Kilwins opened nineteen new locations in 2025. That gives you a sense of momentum, even without the base.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find the chief executive in our sources, which is unusual. We did find two senior appointments. In May 2025, Kilwins appointed Brad Williams as vice president of franchise operations. And in August 2026, it named Kelli Schroeder as chief development officer. In franchising, the chief development officer is typically the person responsible for selling new franchises and opening new territories.

speaker: NORA
text: So the visible hires are about growth and operations.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Franchise development and franchise operations. Not technology, not data, not digital. That tells you where management attention has been focused, at least publicly. That isn't a criticism. For a franchise brand in growth mode, those are the right first hires. But it's relevant to the AI story.

speaker: NORA
text: And the brand recognition?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the standout. In June 2026, Kilwins was named USA TODAY's number one best dessert treat chain in a reader vote. And in October 2026, it celebrated National Dessert Day with a sweepstakes. Reader polls and sweepstakes are classic consumer brand marketing. They rely on, and build, awareness.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk ownership. What do we know?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the twenty-third of February 2023, Levine Leichtman announced it had acquired Kilwins, describing it as a leading franchisor brand of chocolate, ice cream and confectionery products. The firm's own blog headline at the time was "LLCP scoops up storied ice cream shop Kilwins", which I enjoy. We didn't find who the seller was or the terms of the deal.

speaker: NORA
text: And what was the plan?

speaker: JAMES
text: Franchise Times ran two headlines. One said "Iconic Kilwins Chocolates to expand nationwide under new owners Levine Leichtman". Another said "Big growth push for legacy brand Kilwins under Levine Leichtman". We didn't read the articles, but the headlines tell the story. A beloved regional brand, now with private equity backing, pushing for national growth.

speaker: NORA
text: So, about three years and nine months into the hold.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right, as we record. And what we can see in that period is a steady stream of expansion announcements. In May 2025, Kilwins announced ten new Texas locations. In June 2025, a planned location in Austin's East Village development for early 2026. There's an announcement about expanding into the greater Houston market. A plan to debut in Arizona with more than twenty stores. And in February 2026, a new shop in the village centre of Burr Ridge, Illinois, outside Chicago.

speaker: NORA
text: What does a private equity owner typically do with a legacy franchise brand like this?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, the playbook tends to look similar across the industry. Strengthen the franchise sales and support teams, which matches the development and operations hires we've seen. Sign multi-unit deals with experienced operators in new regions, which matches the Texas and Arizona announcements. Refresh marketing and invest in brand awareness, which fits the reader rankings and sweepstakes. And professionalise the supply chain, which for Kilwins means the central production side. We can't see inside the company, so this is our reading of the visible signals, not a description of its actual plan.

speaker: NORA
text: And the risk in that playbook?

speaker: JAMES
text: Growing faster than the support system can handle, and diluting what made the brand special in the first place. A heritage brand that feels like a chain loses some of its charm. Getting the balance right between consistency and that local, small-town feel is, in our view, the central brand challenge for Kilwins.

speaker: NORA
text: Any acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: None found. Like several franchise companies we've covered, the growth appears to be organic, through selling new franchises.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned closures in your notes.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and I want to be careful with these. There are local news reports of a Kilwins in downtown Grand Rapids, Michigan, closing, and then a separate report of it being back open. And a report of a Kilwins store closing at a shopping and dining development called LaCenterra in Katy, Texas. We don't have dates for any of these, so they might be old. Our read is that every franchise system has stores that close, and the reopening in Grand Rapids is a reminder that these stories are often more complicated than a headline. But it's a reminder that unit performance can be uneven.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about what Kilwins actually sells, and why people buy it.

speaker: JAMES
text: The core categories are chocolates, fudge, ice cream and confections. Think boxed chocolates, chocolate-dipped treats, slabs of fudge cut to order, ice cream in cones and cups, and seasonal specialities. And, as of August 2026, an exclusive new waffle cone.

speaker: NORA
text: It's a very sensory product.

speaker: JAMES
text: Hugely. In this kind of shop generally, the smell, the look of the display, watching treats being made or dipped, the waffle cones being pressed, are all part of the appeal. It's retail theatre. You're not just buying a product, you're buying a small experience. We couldn't confirm from our sources exactly what's made in each Kilwins shop versus centrally, so I won't claim specifics, but the experience is clearly central to the brand.

speaker: NORA
text: And who's the customer?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have Kilwins customer data, so this is our inference from the category and the store locations. I'd describe three broad types. First, the treat-seeker, someone strolling past who wants an ice cream or a piece of fudge right now. Second, the gift buyer, someone buying a box of chocolates for a host, a holiday, a birthday or a thank-you. And third, the tourist, who's on holiday and wants a treat and maybe something to take home.

speaker: NORA
text: And those overlap.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. A tourist might buy an ice cream and a box of fudge to take home as a gift. The location matters enormously. Downtown main streets, resort towns, lifestyle shopping centres, places with foot traffic and people in a relaxed, spend-a-little-on-a-treat mood. That's why new developments like the Austin East Village or Burr Ridge's village centre make sense as sites.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there something special about Michigan and fudge?

speaker: JAMES
text: There is, as general background. Northern Michigan has a long tradition of fudge shops in its resort towns, most famously on Mackinac Island, where fudge has been a tourist staple for generations. Locals have even been known to call summer visitors "fudgies", because so many of them leave carrying a box. Kilwins grew up in that culture. So when it opens in Texas or Arizona, it's exporting not just a product but a bit of northern Michigan summer.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a nice story to tell customers.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a great story, and heritage stories sell in confectionery. The challenge is that in Phoenix or Austin, most people won't have that memory. Some will, the ones who've holidayed in Michigan, and those are valuable customers. For everyone else, the store has to win them over on product and experience alone.

speaker: NORA
text: What does a gift purchase look like economically?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, gifts tend to carry bigger baskets than an impulse treat. Someone buying a cone spends a few dollars. Someone buying a holiday gift box, or several, for family and colleagues, spends much more. Gifting is also less weather-dependent than ice cream. So a shop with a strong gifting business is more resilient through the year. That's why seasonal boxed chocolate and corporate gifting matter so much in this category, even if the ice cream queue is what you see in July.

speaker: NORA
text: And the calendar?

speaker: JAMES
text: In confectionery generally, the calendar is everything. There are big gifting moments, Valentine's Day, Easter, Mother's Day, the winter holidays, and big ice cream seasons, mainly summer. A shop in a resort town might do a huge share of its business in a few summer months. A shop in a suburban centre might be steadier but peak around holidays. The product mix shifts with the season too. More ice cream in summer, more boxed chocolate in winter.

speaker: NORA
text: So the demand pattern is incredibly variable.

speaker: JAMES
text: By location, by season, by day of the week and by weather. A hot sunny Saturday in July is a completely different business from a cold Tuesday in February. And that variability is exactly where we'll find the AI opportunity.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the business model. How does Kilwins make money?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: As with any franchisor, and this is general knowledge about franchising, Kilwins earns money from franchise fees when new shops open and ongoing royalties based on store sales. What makes Kilwins a little different from a pure restaurant franchise is the central production piece. If the company makes chocolates and other products centrally and supplies them to stores, it also earns money on those products. That's vertical integration.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: What are the advantages of that?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: Consistency, first. A Kilwins chocolate in Texas should taste the same as one in Michigan. Central production makes that much easier. Second, scale. A central facility can buy ingredients in bulk and run efficient production. Third, product innovation. New recipes and items can be developed and rolled out centrally. And for the franchisor, it's an additional profit stream.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: And the disadvantages?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: Planning. A central facility has to decide what to make, and how much, before stores order it. Make too much and you have stock that may go stale or need discounting. Make too little and stores run out of best-sellers during peak season. And the further the stores are from Michigan, the longer the supply chain, and the more you need to plan ahead. With nineteen new openings in 2025 and expansion into Texas and Arizona, that planning problem gets bigger every year.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: And the franchisees?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: They're running the shops day to day. Ordering from the central supply, making some items in store presumably, staffing, serving, managing their local marketing. Their success depends on picking the right location, staffing well, especially in peak seasons, and ordering the right mix of products. We don't have franchisee economics for Kilwins, so I'll leave it there.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: How does the franchisor know what's happening in the stores?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a really important question, and in our view a gap in many franchise systems. The franchisor sees what each store orders from central supply, and it sees royalty reports based on sales. But it may not see detailed, real-time data on what each store sells by item, by hour, by day. That depends on the point-of-sale systems and the data-sharing terms in the franchise agreements. We don't know Kilwins' setup. But the gap between headquarters' view and the store's reality is a classic franchise challenge.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: And the people?
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot of seasonal and part-time staff, especially in resort locations. That's general knowledge for the category. Summer staffing in a tourist town is famously hard. The shop needs lots of people for a few busy months, and has to train them quickly. That's a franchisee problem, but it's also a brand problem, because the experience depends on those staff.
chapter: The franchise model and central production

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the market?

speaker: JAMES
text: We have one broad figure and a lot of gaps. The National Confectioners Association reported that US confectionery sales surpassed fifty-four billion dollars in 2024. We saw that as a headline. But that's all confectionery, including chocolate bars and candy sold in supermarkets, not chocolate shops specifically. There's an industry research series on US chocolate shops, but we couldn't see the figure. And we didn't find a reliable growth rate for chocolate retail.

speaker: NORA
text: So, big category, unknown niche.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's fair. And the niche is a mix of confectionery retail, ice cream shops and gifting, which makes it hard to size anyway.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: The closest direct comparison is Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory. It's a public company, listed on the Nasdaq, with franchised chocolate stores plus a factory, so a similar model. It reported preliminary results for its fiscal year 2026, which we didn't read. Being public, it's a useful benchmark for the economics of this kind of business, for anyone who wants to dig in.

speaker: NORA
text: What can you learn from Rocky Mountain Chocolate Factory being public?

speaker: JAMES
text: Quite a lot, in principle, for anyone studying this model. A public company has to explain its business in its filings: how many franchised and company stores it has, what it earns from royalties versus selling product to franchisees, how its factory performs, how store openings and closures are trending, and what's happening with costs like cocoa. We didn't read its latest results, so I won't quote any. But if you wanted to understand the economics of a franchised chocolate business with central production, those filings are the closest public proxy for Kilwins, with the obvious caution that two companies can perform very differently.

speaker: NORA
text: And See's?

speaker: JAMES
text: See's Candies is a well-known chocolate retailer, which, as general background, is owned by Berkshire Hathaway. It's more focused on premium boxed chocolates, with a different store format. A business database lists it as a Kilwins comparison. The same database lists others: Ziegenfelder, Milkshake Factory, Bon Bon Bon and Gertrude Hawk. We didn't verify their models or ownership, so I won't characterise them in detail.

speaker: NORA
text: And then every ice cream shop on every main street.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. In practice, Kilwins competes for a treat purchase with all sorts of options: local ice cream parlours, national ice cream chains, coffee shops with pastries, bakeries, independent chocolatiers. On the gifting side, with online gift retailers and supermarket chocolates. The competitive set is wide.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there anything AI-related in the category?

speaker: JAMES
text: A couple of signals, neither directly competing with Kilwins. Dairy Queen has been expanding a test of voice AI in its drive-thrus, according to a financial news headline. And a company called Generation Next Franchise Brands has robotic ice cream and frozen yogurt vending machines. Those show AI and automation entering ice cream retail. Neither is evidence of anything at Kilwins.

speaker: NORA
text: Would a robot ice cream machine ever threaten a Kilwins?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not directly, in my view. Nobody goes to a robot for the experience of a resort-town fudge shop. But automation can change the economics of the quick ice cream purchase, in airports or malls, say. The bigger point is that the category is starting to experiment, and customer expectations around ordering and convenience will shift.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the stock-take. Where is Kilwins with AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: As far as public evidence goes, nowhere visible. We found no Kilwins AI product, no AI partnership, no AI or data hire. Searching for Kilwins and AI returned unrelated results. The visible senior hires are in franchise development and operations. And standard digital tools, an online store and analytics, are what we'd expect, but we couldn't verify the specifics.

speaker: NORA
text: Is that bad?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not necessarily. Plenty of excellent consumer businesses haven't made public AI moves, and something could be happening behind the scenes that just isn't announced. And a confectionery franchise isn't a software company. Its success depends on product quality, locations and franchisee execution far more than on AI. But it does mean Kilwins is starting from a low base, and that's what makes the opportunity interesting.

speaker: NORA
text: There's a loyalty programme, isn't there?

speaker: JAMES
text: We've seen references to a Kilwins Club loyalty programme, but we couldn't confirm it in our sources, so I'd treat it as unverified. If it exists, and if it captures customer purchase data, that would be a useful foundation for personalisation. That's a big if.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the broader point you raised, about commodity tools?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Loyalty and customer relationship tools for online retailers are now widely available as off-the-shelf apps on platforms like Shopify. You can buy a loyalty programme in an afternoon. So having one isn't a differentiator. What matters is what you do with the data. That's true for Kilwins and for any consumer brand.

speaker: NORA
text: What would a typical franchisor at this stage have, in terms of technology?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, and this is not specific to Kilwins, a franchise system like this usually has a point-of-sale system in each store, an ordering system for franchisees to buy from central supply, an e-commerce site for online orders and gifts, some email marketing, and basic analytics. Often those systems were added at different times and don't talk to each other well. The data exists in pieces. The first AI job is frequently not AI at all, it's stitching those pieces together so you can see what's actually happening.

speaker: NORA
text: That sounds like the unglamorous part.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and it's where most of the value starts. You can't forecast demand for a product if you can't see, by store and by day, how much of it sold. Once that data is flowing, even simple models can do a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: So if Kilwins were to start, where should it start?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not with a chatbot, in my view. The highest value is behind the counter, in planning. That's what we'll get into with our walk-through.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. An invented franchisee, a hypothetical shop.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's call her Lauren. She owns two Kilwins shops, one in a lakeside resort town and one in a suburban lifestyle centre about an hour away. It's early July. A heatwave is forecast for the weekend, there's a festival in the resort town on Saturday, and the suburban centre has a summer concert on Friday night.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Old way first.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: On Monday, Lauren sits down with last year's sales, if she has them handy, and her gut feeling. She thinks: hot weekend, festival, I'll need a lot of ice cream at the resort shop, and more waffle cones. She places her order from central supply, guessing quantities. She schedules staff, calling in extra summer workers for Saturday. For the suburban shop, she guesses the concert will help a bit on Friday evening.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then what happens?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: In the version where it goes wrong, the festival is even busier than she expected. By three on Saturday afternoon, the resort shop has run out of the two most popular ice cream flavours and the new waffle cones. Customers are disappointed, the queue thins out, she loses sales on her biggest day of the year. Meanwhile, the suburban shop overestimated the concert, and has too much stock of a seasonal item that will need to be discounted.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And at headquarters?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: At the central production facility, they've seen orders from dozens of stores, each guessing in their own way. Some over-order, some under-order. Production planners try to anticipate summer demand across the whole system, but they're aggregating a lot of guesses. Some products sell out across the system while others pile up.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Now the AI version.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: On Monday, Lauren opens a planning tool provided by Kilwins. It shows a suggested order for each shop, by product, for the coming week. It's based on her stores' sales history, the weather forecast, the local events calendar, the time of year, and what similar stores in similar locations sold in similar conditions. It flags: resort shop, Saturday, expect very high ice cream demand, consider extra stock of the top flavours and waffle cones. Suburban shop, Friday, modest uplift from the concert.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And she can override it.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Of course. She knows things the system doesn't. Maybe the festival has moved to a different street this year, further from her shop. She adjusts. The tool also suggests staffing: how many people she'll need, hour by hour, at each shop. She uses it to plan her summer workers' shifts.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And headquarters?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: This is where it gets powerful. The central facility doesn't just see orders. It sees the forecast for every store, built the same way. So it can plan production for the whole system weeks ahead, knowing that a heatwave across the Midwest will spike ice cream demand, or that Valentine's Day orders in Texas will look different from Michigan. Fewer stockouts in stores, less waste at the centre.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And at the end of the weekend?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Actual sales flow back into the system, including what sold out and when. The forecast learns. Next festival, next heatwave, it's a little better. That's the learning loop we've talked about throughout this series. And notice, again, the AI isn't replacing Lauren's judgment or the production planners'. It's giving them a far better starting point.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What about the person at headquarters? Give me their view.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's call her Grace, a production planner at the central facility. In the old world, Grace's week starts with a pile of franchisee orders and her own seasonal plan. She knows Valentine's Day is coming, she knows roughly how much the system sold last year, but she doesn't know how the ten new Texas stores will behave, because they have no history. So she builds in a buffer, which means extra stock, which means more risk of waste or markdowns if she's wrong.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And with forecasting?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Grace sees a forecast for every store, including new ones, which are modelled on similar existing stores until they build their own history. She can see that a cold snap in the Midwest might shift demand from ice cream to chocolate, or that Arizona stores peak at different times from Michigan ones. She plans production runs and ingredient purchases with more confidence and less buffer. When cocoa is expensive, that buffer is real money.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let me do a second, quicker one. A gift buyer.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call him Ben. He visited a Kilwins on holiday in Michigan last summer and bought fudge. Now it's December, he lives in Arizona, and there's a new Kilwins near him, but he doesn't know that. In the old world, he might never come back to the brand.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And with AI?
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: If Ben signed up to a loyalty programme or bought online, and agreed to hear from Kilwins, a personalised message could tell him: there's now a Kilwins twenty minutes from you, here's the fudge you bought last summer, and here's a holiday gift box. That's not sophisticated AI. It's using data well. But it connects a tourist memory to a local shop, which is exactly the bridge Kilwins needs as it expands into new states.
chapter: A summer Saturday, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's be specific about the challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, data. If Kilwins doesn't have consistent, detailed store-level sales data from its franchisees, every AI idea we've discussed is harder. Getting that data may require changes to point-of-sale systems and franchise agreements, and franchisees need a reason to agree. That's a foundational challenge, and we don't know where Kilwins stands on it.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, expansion risk. Moving from a Michigan heartland into Texas, Arizona and Illinois means entering markets where some customers know the brand from holidays and many don't. The closures in Grand Rapids and Katy, whatever their dates and causes, are a reminder that not every location works. Site selection matters enormously in this business.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, seasonality and staffing. Resort shops in particular have intense peaks. Staffing them with enough trained people, and keeping quality consistent, is hard. And new markets in hotter climates, like Arizona and Texas, may have different seasonal patterns from Michigan, which the system has to learn.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, input costs. Cocoa, dairy and sugar prices can be volatile. This is general category knowledge, not something our sources quantify for Kilwins. When cocoa prices spike, a chocolate business either absorbs the cost or raises prices. Better forecasting and less waste help cushion that.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, consumer trends. There's a broader question about how consumers feel about sugary, indulgent treats over time. We didn't find data quantifying any shift for this category. Our view is that treats and gifts are resilient, people celebrate and indulge in good times and bad, but it's worth watching.

speaker: NORA
text: You haven't mentioned the lack of tech leadership.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd add it as a sixth. With no visible technology, data or digital leader, any AI programme needs an owner. That doesn't have to mean hiring a chief AI officer. It could be a strong operations or supply chain leader who champions forecasting. But someone has to own it.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay. Opportunities. Where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first and biggest is the one from our walk-through: connect store-level sales to central production with demand and inventory forecasting. Kilwins makes product centrally for many franchised stores. A forecast that feeds production planning scales across every new opening. The value levers are margin, through less waste and fewer stockouts, and some labour at store level. In our view, that's the cleanest link between AI and the profit and loss in a multi-unit franchise business.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, franchisee staffing and demand planning. Forecast store-level labour needs from local traffic, weather and tourist seasons. That helps franchisees schedule better, especially in summer. It's a direct benefit to them, which matters for adoption.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, personalised marketing. Shift from broad promotions like sweepstakes and national days to targeted offers, using loyalty and online purchase data, with consent. Like Ben's example: connecting a tourist who bought in Michigan to a new store near home.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, pricing and product mix. Test changes on premium items, like the new waffle cone, or on seasonal boxes. Which items should be in a gift box, at which price, in which market? Modest AI tools can help analyse that from sales data.

speaker: NORA
text: Fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, smarter site selection. Use data from existing successful shops, foot traffic, tourism, demographics, nearby attractions, to prioritise new locations that look like the winners. With twenty-plus stores planned for Arizona and ten for Texas, getting site selection right is worth a lot. AI-assisted site selection is a well-established tool in retail.

speaker: NORA
text: What about franchisee support and training? You mentioned the seasonal staff.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good sixth. With nineteen openings a year, Kilwins is onboarding lots of new franchisees and their teams, many in states far from Petoskey. An AI assistant trained on the operations manual and recipes, available on a tablet in the shop, could answer "how do I set up the new waffle cone display" or "what's the procedure for tempering this batch" at any hour. That reduces the load on the franchise operations team, which, as we've seen, now has a dedicated vice president. It's a modest, low-risk use of AI, and it helps seasonal staff get up to speed faster.

speaker: NORA
text: And online?

speaker: JAMES
text: Online gifting is a seventh. People who discover Kilwins on holiday may want to order from home later, especially at the holidays. Smarter recommendations on the online store, like "customers who bought this fudge also sent this gift box", are standard e-commerce tools, but they need good data and decent product content to work.

speaker: NORA
text: And beyond that?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two more. Corporate and gifting orders, using the national brand and the seasonal calendar. Businesses buying holiday gifts for clients, for example. And, more speculatively, acquisitions of other confectionery brands that could use the same central production base. That's our inference, not anything announced.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months?

speaker: JAMES
text: Store-to-production demand and inventory forecasting. It touches the most money, it benefits both the franchisor and the franchisees, and it scales with every new store. And it builds the data foundation that every other opportunity, staffing, personalisation, site selection, will need.

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run it? First hundred days.

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: find out what data exists. What do the point-of-sale systems in stores capture? What does headquarters actually receive, how often, and at what level of detail? What does central production use to plan today? Appoint an owner, probably someone from supply chain or operations, working closely with the franchise operations team. And recruit a group of willing franchisees, say ten to fifteen shops, with a mix of resort, suburban and new-market locations.

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?

speaker: JAMES
text: Build a simple forecast for the pilot shops. It doesn't need to be cutting-edge AI at first. Sales history, day of week, season, weather and local events will get you a long way. Run it in shadow mode: give franchisees a suggested order alongside their usual process, and let them choose. Track what they ordered, what the forecast suggested and what actually sold. In parallel, give central production a view of the pilot forecasts.

speaker: NORA
text: And sixty to a hundred?

speaker: JAMES
text: Compare. Was the forecast closer to actual sales than the franchisees' own orders? Did stockouts and waste fall where franchisees followed it? Did the franchisees find it useful? If yes, plan a rollout timed for the next major season, holiday or summer, and work out how to bring more stores' data into the system. If not, learn why and iterate.

speaker: NORA
text: And the measure?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two numbers. Stockouts on top-selling items during peak periods, and waste or markdowns as a share of product supplied. If both fall, franchisees make more money and so does the franchisor.

speaker: NORA
text: Second-best bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Data-assisted site selection for the expansion. With dozens of new stores planned, every bad site avoided is worth a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: What can other businesses learn from Kilwins?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four. First, you don't have to start with a chatbot. For many businesses, the most valuable AI is invisible to customers. It's in planning, forecasting and supply. Kilwins' biggest opportunity is behind the counter, not in front of it.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, data comes before AI. If you don't have consistent, detailed data on what you sell, where and when, AI can't help much. For franchise businesses especially, getting store-level data flowing to the centre is step one, and it's often a commercial negotiation as much as a technical project.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, a strong brand buys you time but not immunity. Kilwins has wonderful brand recognition, a number one reader ranking, heritage, a loyal following. That's a big advantage. But as it expands into new markets and competitors get smarter, brand alone won't guarantee every new shop succeeds. Operational excellence, increasingly supported by data, matters more as you scale.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, start AI where the franchisee benefits. In a franchise system, the franchisor can't force adoption. Choose AI projects that make franchisees' lives easier and their shops more profitable, and adoption follows. A forecast that saves a franchisee from running out of ice cream on the busiest day of summer is an easy sell.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's run the risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, franchisee economics. If store closures or franchisee churn rise, the growth model weakens. Two, expansion into markets where the brand is less known. Three, input cost volatility in cocoa, dairy and sugar. Four, consumer shifts in attitudes to sugary treats, which we can't quantify. Five, AI-driven discovery. As more people ask AI assistants for recommendations or gift ideas, traffic might be routed away from brand websites and promotions, unless Kilwins shows up well in those systems.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Nearly four years in, the growth story is visible: new states, new openings, a strong brand ranking, a new development leader. The next step, in our view, is to show that the growth is profitable and repeatable, which is exactly what better data and forecasting would demonstrate.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, the Texas and Arizona openings. Are the planned stores actually opening, and on time? Second, any technology, data or digital leadership hire, which would signal investment in this area. Third, any announcement of a loyalty, app or digital ordering initiative. And fourth, any sign of AI in production or planning, even a modest one.

speaker: NORA
text: And what's missing from the public record?

speaker: JAMES
text: Almost everything you'd want for a proper analysis. Founding year confirmed, chief executive, store count, revenue, unit economics, what's made centrally versus in store, and how data flows between stores and headquarters. If you work in this business, you know these things, and they'd change the picture.

speaker: NORA
text: James, this is our last episode. Before the quick-fire round, I want to step back. Thirty companies. What have we learned across the whole portfolio?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out three themes, and I'll stick to what we've actually seen in the episodes rather than inventing anything new.

speaker: NORA
text: Go on.

speaker: JAMES
text: The first is buy-and-build. Again and again, these companies grow by acquisition as well as organically. BigHand assembled a suite of products through acquisitions and then bought the AI pricing company Ayora. Club Champion bought TXG in Canada and Golf Principles in the UK. And the recurring lesson was that buying is quick and integrating is slow. Nineteen months for Club Champion to merge the TXG brand. A multi-step integration for BigHand's pricing agent. The companies that do buy-and-build well treat integration as the real work.

speaker: NORA
text: And the companies like Kilwins, Shipley and SEV, which seem to grow organically?

speaker: JAMES
text: They're the counterpoint. They grow by opening new units, through franchising or new clinics. That's a different discipline, all about site selection, operator quality and support capacity. But it shares the same truth: growth is the easy headline, consistency at scale is the hard part.

speaker: NORA
text: Second theme?

speaker: JAMES
text: Buying versus building AI. Very few of these companies are building AI from scratch, and that's mostly sensible. SEV's AI comes from its software vendor, Zenoti. Shipley's ordering assistant was reported to be powered by a vendor, Saivory. BigHand partnered with Ayora and then bought it. Club Champion launched its own named Co-Pilot back in 2023. The lesson I'd draw is that buying the AI is rarely the advantage on its own. The advantage is in using it well, owning the data and the customer relationship, and continuing to invest after launch. Being first isn't a moat. Being best at using it might be.

speaker: NORA
text: And the third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Franchise adoption. Several of the companies we covered are franchise or multi-unit businesses: Shipley, Kilwins, SEV with its clinics, Schülerhilfe with its owned and franchised tutoring centres, among others. In those businesses, AI adoption isn't a decision headquarters makes alone. Franchisees and site managers have to see the benefit in their own shops. The most promising AI in those systems is the kind delivered from the centre, like Shipley's assistant on its website, or the kind that obviously helps the operator, like the forecasting we discussed today.

speaker: NORA
text: Was there anything that surprised you, across the whole series?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two things. First, how often the best AI opportunity turned out to be in operations rather than in a customer-facing product. Forecasting at Kilwins and Shipley, component planning at Club Champion, retention at SEV. The public conversation about AI is dominated by chatbots, but in these businesses the money is often in planning. Second, how much governance lagged. Across several companies, we found no public AI policy or security statement, even where customers were sharing sensitive data. That's an easy gap to close, and in our view it will increasingly matter to customers and to future buyers.

speaker: NORA
text: And for anyone running a business who's listened to all thirty?

speaker: JAMES
text: Ask the boring question first. Where do we lose money through guesswork? Over-production, missed calls, mispriced work, wrong stock in the wrong place. That's usually where the first good AI project lives.

speaker: NORA
text: And if you had to sum up the whole series in one sentence?

speaker: JAMES
text: The companies that will win with AI aren't the ones with the flashiest announcements, they're the ones that put it where the value is, measure whether customers actually use it, and keep improving it.

speaker: NORA
text: And honestly, the other thing we learned is how often the public record runs out.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's true. In episode after episode, we had to say "not publicly known". Revenue, headcount, adoption numbers. Which is why, when a company does publish a real number, like Shipley's one in four, it stands out so much.

speaker: NORA
text: One last quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: Kilwins: chocolate shop or ice cream shop?

speaker: JAMES
text: Both, and the gift shop too. That mix is the strength.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: A heritage brand people vote for, plus central production.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: No visible data or AI foundation, and a thin public record.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Forecasting that connects store sales to central production.

speaker: NORA
text: Will a robot ever make a better fudge shop?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. But software can make sure the fudge shop doesn't run out on a Saturday.

speaker: NORA
text: Favourite company of the series?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'm not allowed to pick favourites. But the one with a real adoption number made my job easiest.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing every company in this series should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pick one AI use case tied to a number on the profit and loss, and measure it honestly.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist, about the whole portfolio?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. Almost every company we covered has a clear, practical AI opportunity. The gap is execution, not ideas.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary of today. Kilwins is a chocolate, fudge, ice cream and confectionery franchisor headquartered in Petoskey, Michigan, with central production behind its shops, owned by Levine Leichtman since February 2023. It opened nineteen locations in 2025, is expanding into Texas, Arizona and Illinois, named a new chief development officer in August 2026, and was voted the number one dessert chain by USA TODAY readers in June 2026. Much of the public record is thin, and we found no public evidence of AI. That makes its biggest opportunity clear: connect store sales to central production with forecasting, cut waste and stockouts, help franchisees staff their busy seasons, and build the data foundation for everything else, while the expansion tests whether a much-loved regional brand can succeed nationally.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the lesson is that the most valuable AI is often the kind customers never see.

speaker: NORA
text: And that brings us to the end of Portfolio Deep Dives. Thirty companies, from law firm software and expert witnesses to golf clubs, donuts, laser clinics and fudge. Thank you so much to everyone who followed along, all thirty episodes. We hope you learned as much as we did.

speaker: JAMES
text: Thank you for listening, and for putting up with all our caveats about what isn't publicly known. It's been a pleasure. Take care, and go and get yourself a treat.
